one_liner: Asynchronous C++ logging library, drastically lower caller-side latency than std::fstream/fprintf and other async loggers.
what_it_does: Reckless is a printf-style, type-safe logging library. Call sites push arguments onto a lockless queue and return immediately; a dedicated background thread formats and writes them. API is not a drop-in for fstream/fprintf: you construct a writer (file_writer, stdout_writer, or custom) and a policy_log/severity_log template, then call typed write/debug/info/warn/error methods with printf-like format strings.
how_it_is_fast: Call site only pushes args onto a lockless MPSC ring buffer (mpsc_ring_buffer.hpp) shared with the writer thread, so the common case costs about one function call with no kernel transition, no lock, and no formatting or I/O on the caller's thread. Formatting and writing happen entirely on the background thread, and bursts of queued entries are batched into fewer I/O operations. Uses a home-grown float-to-string routine (template_formatter) instead of the standard library's, trading some accuracy for speed.
when_to_use: Latency-sensitive hot paths that log frequently but can tolerate async/eventual persistence
Single-threaded or lightly-threaded workloads where formatting cost on a shared background thread won't bottleneck
Windows or Linux targets on x86-family hardware; C++11-only codebases
Willing to vendor/pin an unmaintained MIT library instead of using an actively developed logger
Need low overhead specifically vs. synchronous std::fstream/fprintf-with-flush logging
when_not_to_use: Need macOS/BSD support (README: OS X unsupported, BSD only 'on the roadmap')
High log-argument volume from many parallel threads, since all formatting funnels through one background thread (README calls this out as a scalability limit)
Passing pointers/references to short-lived data without ensuring they outlive the flush (dangling-pointer risk by design)
Need guaranteed-precise float formatting: custom float-to-string algorithm mismatches the exact/shortest round-trip representation for roughly 0.6% of values per the manual's own stats
Want an actively maintained project: last commit 2021-04-10, open ThreadSanitizer data-race report (#35) unresolved

integration.form: static lib (built via Make/CMake/Visual Studio; not header-only)
integration.dependencies: pthread (POSIX threads) on Linux; no other third-party deps for core library
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (CMakeLists.txt sets CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD 11); GCC-compatible compiler or MSVC/Visual Studio
integration.platforms: Windows and Linux only; no macOS/OS X, BSD listed as roadmap-only; no stated architecture restriction beyond x86 cache-line-size assumptions in the buffer sizing docs
integration.thread_safety: Multiple threads may call write/debug/info/warn/error concurrently (lockless input queue); worker_thread() access for priority/affinity tuning is documented as unsafe to misuse (moving/detaching it breaks the library); an open issue (#35) reports ThreadSanitizer-flagged data races the maintainer has not resolved
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: not source-compatible with std::fstream/fprintf; requires constructing a writer + policy_log/severity_log object and using its typed write methods instead of ostream operators or printf

gotchas: Passing log arguments by pointer/reference requires the referenced data to stay valid until the log is flushed or closed; prefer std::string/shared_ptr/unique_ptr for dynamic data
Crash safety requires explicit handling (panic_flush/crash_handler) since unflushed async data can be lost on crash, same class of issue as buffered fprintf but easier to overlook
Custom float-to-string formatter is not always the shortest round-trip representation: manual reports 98.5% exact match and 99.4% correct-but-sometimes-longer over 100M random values
worker_thread() exposes the internal std::thread for OS-level tuning (priority/affinity) but destructive operations on it (move/detach) will break the logger
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No siblings catalogued yet in this category target std::fstream/fprintf directly the way reckless does; CPath and FastReader address filesystem traversal and file reads, not logging, so they aren't substitutes for this use case.
verified_claims_summary: First-party benchmarks (doc/performance.md, gcc 7.3.0, AMD Ryzen 7 2700X @3.7GHz, libstdc++) show reckless's caller-side latency far below std::fstream (flushed per line) and fprintf (fflush per call): about 41-44x lower under light periodic load, and up to ~5720x lower than fstream in the disk-I/O scenario, though this compares an async design against baselines that synchronously flush every line, not raw I/O throughput.
status_note: Abandoned: last commit on master 2021-04-10, no newer maintenance activity found; MIT licensed and small enough to vendor, but an unresolved ThreadSanitizer data-race report (#35) and a still-open VS2019 compile-error issue (#45) are unpatched.
